#3955. Talking Point: As A Parent, What Worries You Most About Gaming?

Nintendo's guide aims to highlight the benefits

Over the summer, I replayed Ocarina of Time (1998) with my kids. I hadn't intended to, but it dawned on me that once the gorgeous remake landed, the original's visible polygons might not hold the same appeal for them. It was selfish, really, but I wanted them to experience the original magic as I did.

I held the pad but let them direct me, staying silent or feigning ignorance about puzzle solutions, letting them speculate and point out chests and switches I'd intentionally run past, involving them in an adventure they don't quite have the dexterity to control themselves.

I worried their attention might wander while watching for 30-60 minutes at a time, and I don't want to be that parent, forcing something I loved on my disinterested kids ("What do you mean 'Thunderbirds is boring'?!"). I was ready to pull the cord if they didn't take to it.

But no! They were pointing and problem-solving alongside me, jumping up and down, utterly engaged and loving the story and our shared experience.

Beyond the screen, Ocarina provoked laughter over dinner, and discussion about why characters reacted as they did, the cause and effect of actions, and the resulting emotions. Car journeys suddenly had a new soundtrack accompaniment, and the game's themes would come up while drawing or playing with Lego or finding a 'Deku' stick out on a walk. It became a rich source of inspiration for their imaginations, and a springboard to conversation and closeness with my kids. A fantastic family adventure we'll remember for years to come.

It's such a shame, then, when you see parents whose kids love games struggle to recognise the benefits and sheer joy they can bring, and potentially miss out on family experiences like mine. For something so ubiquitous and so fun, gaming can create real tension in the home and throw up generational barriers that take time and understanding to break down.

And with all the online concerns and other ills of the modern age, it's easy to see why some parents might perceive games as a dead-end, dangerous time sink that needs to be contained and quarantined, like fast food or social media.

According to a recent Ofcom report, 88% of children aged 3-17 in the UK play games on some form of device, and given Nintendo's evergreen, all-ages remit to deliver surprise and delight, addressing concerns of gaming-cautious guardians is something the company is keen on, beyond the bare minimum of secure account systems and Parental Control tools.

So that'll be why they've partnered up with Andy Robertson, founder of the Family Gaming Database and longtime friend of the site, for the recently published Parent's Guide to Gaming with Confidence.

Longtime Nintendo Life readers may recognise Andy from the various articles and reviews he's penned for us over the years, or from our partnership with Family Gaming to highlight accessibility information in our reviews and game pages across the network.

Produced in association with Nintendo, in this new guide Andy has also enlisted other experts in the fields of gaming, child psychology, and online safety to help parents of all gaming backgrounds digest the key questions and perhaps reframe how some of them view video games.

The prevalence of online gaming and voice chat worries me a lot. I don't want my kid speaking to strangers or picking up bad language or habits. Everything is so much easier (and tempting) to access than it used to be!

Available as a downloadable PDF, Andy explores common misconceptions and offers sound advice from expert contributors, including child psychologist Dr Amanda Gummer and Dr Catherine Knibbs, a child and adult psychotherapist specialising in online harm.

As you'll see from the breakout boxes on this page, uncertainties about other online players and predatory monetisation systems are the main sources of anxiety for NL staff with kids. "I'm very concerned about exploitative mechanics," says Alex, our senior video producer, "things designed to get their hooks into people's brains and make them dependent, or cough up wads of cash."

According to Ofcom's research, these are common worries:

The biggest type of concern among parents and carers of 3-17-year-olds who play games online is their child talking to strangers through games or via the chat functions (64%). This is followed by concerns about bullying by other players (60%), exposure to inappropriate content such as violence, bad language or disturbing material (59%), and pressure to make in-game purchases (51%).

Dr Knibbs highlights how "digital spaces can feel less familiar" than physical play spaces like playgrounds. The dangers can be less obvious, too, although she stresses that understanding the risks is better than avoidance. "When we learn about the content, the people and the spaces our children are engaging with, we are much better placed to help them navigate those experiences safely and positively."

It's not just about risk assessment, but also realising the potential benefits - and that doesn't require extensive gaming experience. "The goal ISN’T to become a gamer," Andy writes. "It is to better understand the people you care about most." You don't need to have conquered Elden Ring or any other game to participate and 'get' games.

Games with random or chance-based outcomes, especially with microtransactions that encourage you to spend money and try again, are what concern me most. As much as I enjoy it, Pokémon GO is a strong example of this (there’s a reason it was recently bumped up to PEGI 16), but thankfully, there are enough single-player adventures out there (Pokémon included!) that can minimise these often frustrating and FOMO-driven elements for younger players.

Another key point to stress to non-gaming parents might seem almost self-evident, but it's easily overlooked if recognising Mario and Pac-Man represents your sum knowledge of the medium.

For some, even now, 'gaming' remains an arcade-style competition for high scores, and that can create a disconnect between parents with preconceived notions and their kids, who are discovering that games can be so much more.

"A child who is creating, collaborating, problem-solving or connecting with friends is having a very different experience from someone passively consuming content," Dr Amanda Gummer writes in a section of the guide highlighting "one of the most common mistakes parents make" - that all games are essentially the same.

We can all recall 'Wow, games can do this???' moments when the scales fell from our eye. It might have been an emotional beat in Shadow of the Colossus, or a surprising Wii Sports session with grandparents over the holidays; whatever the source, getting the uninitiated to that point is a crucial first step. While it's all notionally 'reading', hopping between Wikipedia articles is obviously not the same as reading a poem or sitting down with James Patterson's latest or doomscrolling social media feeds or taking a crack at Ulysses, and once parents understand that the world of video games is equally expansive, they've got a foundation to build upon.

Andy takes time to break down what he terms "the myth of the isolated gamer" and how, in fact, games can bring families together. Living the Nintendo life as we do, multiplayer has been commonplace for decades, but the lone gamer in the basement/attic stereotype persists.

Likewise — and this has long been a personal bugbear when talking with friends and family — rationing 'screen time' feels like an oversimplification for parents guarding against passive media consumption. Lamenting how young people these days don't get enough fresh air is absolutely valid, and getting out in the park, playground, and beyond is crucial to a child's overall development, but it's not as simple as 'outside=good, inside=bad'. The storytelling, learning, collaboration, creativity, and deep experiences games can offer are enormously valuable.

As Andy points out, "understanding the quality of the experience is often more useful than simply counting the minutes." Bowling in Switch Sports, having the national news on in the background, diving into a Mario world, and throwing Bluey on Disney+ are all different types of 'screen time', each with their own benefits and potential drawbacks.

You may not have noticed, but Nintendo Life has grown recently. Behind the scenes, we've had new additions to the family, with two team members recently joining the ranks of Hookshot Media parentdom.

Across our editorial, video, and management teams, our collective tribe runs the age gamut from newborn to undergrad, so we've got a broad range of experience, making it fairly simple to gauge what's appropriate for our kids, suggest games they might like (or slyly leave them lying around to be 'discovered') while monitoring interactions and steering them towards the all-timers (hi, Ocarina) and, importantly, away from less healthy, obsessive patterns that we may have fallen into in our youth.

And yes, there are certain games, primarily targeting younger gamers, that we wouldn't install on any device in the house.

I don’t worry too much about microtransactions as I will maintain strict control over any potential in-game purchases. However, I dread the day that my daughter gets roped into playing something like Roblox. Substantial, well-made games can offer a lot of value for children, but Roblox is not an example of this.

Authorities in some territories are taking steps to mitigate the potential harm of the aggressive monetisation systems baked into platforms like Roblox. In the last week, the EU published its Digital Fairness Act proposal, which could impact any game featuring in-game purchases in the EU. Among other things, the bloc is seeking to curtail "addictive design", "dark patterns", and predatory monetisation tactics.

The DFA would only affect players in Europe, but regulation that forces real currency prices and lootbox odds to be displayed, those and similar systems defaulting to 'off' for minors, and parental consent being required to activate them are all positive steps.

While legislation could mean big changes for some developers and publishers, it's unlikely to cause Nintendo itself headaches.

With first-party software, in-game purchases are typically limited to DLC expansions or Switch 2 Upgrade Packs, and content-wise, it's a rare Nintendo game that I wouldn't feel comfortable playing with my kids in the room - something our teams over on Push Square and Pure Xbox have to be more cautious about, I'd wager.

My child is too young to play games on their own yet, but we’re having a blast with Mario Kart World’s Free Roam mode. It’s perfect, honestly: beyond the vibrant, fun characters, and chancing upon helicopters, lorries, and UFOs you can play as, seeing them gradually understand the geography of this vast world as you string one P-Switch mission to the next has made one of my favourite ever Mario Kart (and gaming) experiences.

Every kid is different, of course. Some may not be phased at all by a lurching ReDead in Hyrule Castle Town, while others might be kept up at night after glimpsing a creepy icon on the home screen. Handily, Switch's handheld hybrid format does make it easier to take the game away from the living room if, say, you need half an hour with Resident Evil Requiem away from eager eyes, and the console's aforementioned Parental Controls and accompanying app make monitoring the kids' gaming pretty simple.

Communicating to nervous parents not just the risks but the rewards is something we're passionate about on the team, and that's something that Andy's guide does particularly well. "Failure is a part of success," he writes. "Games create safe environments where mistakes are expected. This can help children build resilience without even realising it. Every setback becomes part of learning." Makes me feel better about all the times the dogs got me in Call of Duty.

Gaming with an infant is… difficult! (Try explaining that Fortune's Weave isn't touchscreen to a five-month-old). But I genuinely can't wait until my child is old enough to participate; as cheesy as it is, I think I'm going to well up when she picks her first starter Pokémon.

Confidence is a key term. Naturally, it's in Nintendo's interest to maintain its carefully curated family-friendly image, but giving parents who aren't embedded in the ins and outs of the gaming scene the confidence to engage is a win for the medium and everyone who loves it. A digestible guide like this for game-sceptic family and friends could come in handy over the holidays.

(To be clear, I'm not advocating becoming a gaming missionary at the dinner table and forcing pamphlets on relatives. But, you know, slyly leaving them lying around to be 'discovered' and having Switch Sports Resort ready to go after dessert? A round of golf and some bowling has worked wonders in the past!)

As with anything, a good grasp of the issues is essential, and every parent and child will have their own approaches, preferences, and ideas. For the NL team, though — and for me personally — sharing how games can enrich our family lives regardless of experience and ability is important. By alleviating concerns and highlighting benefits, we can open doors for new players and experience more of those treasured 'Oh, games can do this???' moments together.

What worries you most as a parent? Which games have you played and enjoyed the most with your kids? Let us know your thoughts in the polls below, and feel free to take to the comments to share your experiences and the effect gaming has in your family.

The thing I'm most worried about for our future kids is endless, meaningless games-as-a-service games, like Roblox and Fortnite. There's no story, no curation, and/or no purpose. Not a parent, but I have spent a lot of time around my nieces and nephews and have watched the games they play. They all play Roblox to some extent (it’s even on their parents’ and grandparents’ iPads, and they’re constantly asking for screens whenever they visit family). My biggest concerns with them and gaming for younger audiences in general are the predatory nature of the games and the lack of concern for their safety from almost all involved parties.

The first point is simple: from what I’ve seen, games on Roblox are meant to be as addictive as possible. By getting kids hooked, they’ll want to keep coming back for more. They do this by having instant feedback loops where you feel like you’re accomplishing something great by ticking up a number constantly. And by implementing the cosmetics and currencies, they’ll be tempted to ask for money for Robux. It just feels predatory.

The last part is on the games, but also on parents. I don’t want to say my siblings are not parenting well, but they’re not gamers, so to me, they don’t seem to be monitoring what their kids consume. And Roblox, as we’ve heard in recent news, can be a breeding ground for predators. It feels way too easy for kids to have access to people they can chat with, and unless a parent is actively monitoring every person they chat to, they don’t know if the person on the other end has good motives.

I don’t want to act like online gaming can’t be helpful for kids, and honestly, kids should be able to play online with their friends. But I think it requires a lot more vigilance from their parents. Long gone are the days where an iPad could babysit a kid (a practice I didn’t even like back when iPads were first introduced). Parents need to have an active role in their kids’ development rather than trusting that the media their kids consume will be good for them.

The online stuff is the worry in the main - but that is just the same stuff that is bothersome about the internet generally.

As someone who has raised two kids who are now older teens and gamed their entire life here are my tips:

1. Dictate everything they can play. The likes of Roblox might be predatory but they are also utter balls. That play time is only so high because non-gaming parents use it to keep their kids quiet. You’re already on a Nintendo site and therefore know better. Let them play the classics you grew up with. The best thing you can do for your kids is curate taste in video games.

2. Play with them as much as possible. Get the Wii out the loft and play some Resort with them. If they’re a bit older try some co-op titles. Secret of Mana remains a milestone to this day. If they’re want to play shooters put paintball mode on Perfect Dark and do co-op vs bots.

3. Take time to listen to what they’re interested in as they age. If you’ve done your job right (see part 1) they’ll want to talk to you about games. My youngest is always throwing crazy Zelda theories at me that sound like 2000 era forum posts and it’s wonderful.

4. Play games as a family on a regular basis. Sit down and play Bomberman or Mario Kart together once a week.

#3954. Xbox Is Releasing Two First-Party Expansions In December 2026

December is often a very quiet month for new game releases, and that's particularly going to be the case in 2026 due to GTA 6's arrival and the desire from publishers to get as far away from it as possible, but we've still got the likes of Rayman Legends Retold and Stage Tour to look forward to, along with a couple of first-party Xbox expansions.

In terms of first-party stuff, Xbox is initially releasing a paid DLC pack for Minecraft Dungeons 2 on December 1st called The Humblers Awaken. This DLC is included with the Deluxe Edition of the game if you bought it, and it'll be available separately as well.

You can expect "new quests, unexplored environments, colorful cosmetics, and an expanded arsenal of powerful gear" in The Humblers Awaken, while base game players will also be treated to a free update on the same day, adding in new challenges, weapons and armour.

Then, just a day later, Xbox and Obsidian are releasing a first expansion for The Outer Worlds 2, known as Side Effects Guaranteed. This DLC includes a new narrative story (that'll be concluded in the second part next year), a new region of Elysium Valley to explore, new threats, new perks and an increased level cap.

There's also new weapons, armours, outfits, flaws, a new radio station - you get the picture!

Side Effects Guaranteed will cost $14.99 USD when it arrives on December 2nd, or you'll get it included if you bought either the Premium Edition or Premium Upgrade Edition of The Outer Worlds 2.

Perhaps there's a chance we might get even more from Xbox's first-party studios in December, but as mentioned, it's typically a month where the releases die down. In any case, it's nice to see two expansions on the way very soon!

On this page: Xbox Is Releasing Two First-Party Expansions In December 2026

The Sift is in danger! Something ancient is stirring beneath the ground of the new dimension – a threat that has slumbered for ages and is now beginning to wake. Gather your trusty allies, venture deep into unexplored reaches, take on the not-so-happy humblers, and confront the foes behind their rude awakening!

Side Effects Guaranteed is the first chapter of a two-part expansion for The Outer Worlds 2. A distress signal beckons you and your crew of the Incognito to a derelict ship, where you discover the ship’s crew in suspended animation to keep themselves alive, as they’ve been infected with something that causes explosive cell death. The hunt for a cure leads to Elysium Valley, a brand-new region on Eden.

The game's original worlds keep going from strength to strength

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

MTG Nauctis feels like it's going to repeat history, but in a good way. While Magic: The Gathering's approach to crossovers has met with mixed results, I don't think anyone could argue that its original IP has let the side down in 2026 – and based on everything we've seen so far of the underwater set from MagicCon Atlanta, it should continue that trend into next year.

MTG Nauctis is the first Magic release of 2027, and it's a new, entirely original world set beneath the waves. This is a planet completely covered by ocean, so it's split into distinct zones like the shallows and the dark Abyss, where temperatures fall and pressure is unforgiving. That means it's home to a host of underwater civilizations where Magic: The Gathering's team's creativity is allowed to go wild. However, this is one of the best card games, so it's also the source of fascinating new mechanics.

MTG Nauctis is Magic's first purely underwater set, and it's due to launch on February 5, 2027. It's made up of the usual booster sets, bundles, and four Commander decks. These are all up to pre-order at Amazon.

So much of this is tied to the set's underwater aesthetic. Judging by MTG's own explainer, its magic is heavily tied to the water; air can apparently trap foes or distort vision, for example. Tides may be able to speed your creatures along, and algae can heal or hinder. We don't have in-game examples of these yet, but Magic's own explainer provides a good idea of how it'll all work.

Personally, the thing that fascinates me most is the deeply layered worldbuilding at play here. Besides an entire world of underwater societies like mermaids, sharkfolk, and sea otters (here called 'Pinneons', a species of master artisans who can go between surface and sea), there are also hints at a compelling lost history. For instance, there are humans on Nauctis… and they claim that dry land once existed here, but was lost for reasons unknown. Now they make do as best they can on stilt cities, ships, and submarines that ply the ocean for scavenged goods.

It's one hell of a setup, and I'm already locked in – I can't wait to dive in come February.

#3949. Random: KFC Australia Staging Fake Funeral to Give GTA 6 Fans a 'Legit' Reason to Skip Work

GTA 6 mania has paved the way to some pretty wild headlines over the last couple of years, but now, as we approach the finish line, KFC might have provided the craziest yet.

In Australia, the fast food chain has announced it's holding a fake funeral in order to provide people with a plausible reason to take the day off work. Yes, really.

The company teased the event on social media platforms:

The funeral, for the dearly departed (and completely non-existent) Ann Alibi, will take place on 19th November, 11am AEST at the KFC in Robina, Queensland.

Attendees will be able to enjoy some free chicken at the wake.

Apparently, the service includes "a hearse, coffin, floral tributes, a book of condolences, an order of service and even a heartfelt eulogy delivered by a surprise guest."

If you can't attend in person, a livestream will be broadcast starting at 12pm AEST, and you can still claim that free food via delivery instead.

So, if you're an Aussie looking for an excuse to take 19th November off work, KFC's marketing stunt may be just the ticket.

This isn't the only business reacting to the imminent launch of GTA 6; some, such as Palworld dev Pocketpair, are simply giving employees the time off.

Slay the Spire 2 has a new character—notably, a new character in testing—and as the patch notes themselves point out, that testing will very much be needed: "We expect to make a great number of content and balance changes before the Fool is ready for the main branch."

I decided to hop into the beta branch myself and take her for a whirl, and—yeah, those changes'll have to come. The Fool's central mechanic is her bow and arrow—she can fire an arrow/shoot card to deal damage equal to the card's base damage plus her aim. So if a shoot card deals 15 damage and she has six aim stocked, she'll deal 21.

This is a little busted, because by default, the Fool has 6 aim already put in her bank. Her non-strike starter card, Foolish Shot, already deals a hefty 15 damage for just one energy. With aim, the first time she uses it, it deals a whopping 21 damage, which is a heck of a damage output for the Fool's first round of combat.

The saving grace here is that when a card that fires an arrow is used, that arrow becomes lodged in a target, who gains the Impale status. You can't play any more arrow-based cards until you either Dislodge (another game term, hence the proper nounage) an arrow with a card that dislodges, or until you have more than one arrow.

In my runs, I wasn't able to figure out the latter. But I really didn't need to, because I was one-shotting bosses the whole way up the spire. One card in particular, Repeat Shot, seems borderline broken. While it is a rare, it shoots a target for 20 damage (when upgraded) X times, plus your current aim.

With precious little setup, I was casually knocking (or should I say nocking) out around 78 damage on turn one just by having the card pop into my hand. Add even a little aim generation to your deck, and Repeat Shot solves single-target fights for you. By making them dead.

There are some other interesting mechanics, too, such as a trio of melodies you can activate and trigger other cards off of. Wah Blast, for instance, hits twice if you've got a Cho or Ki melody active. There's also Stretch, which gives you extra block on the usage of your next block card, Sadness, a status card that can be turned into Joy which gives you energy and card draw, and tarot cards via a power called Mythic Form.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

Obviously, she's broken. I absolutely shouldn't be one-card tapping bosses on Act 1 just because I happened to first-turn draw into a single rare card. But she is already very fun, and I look forward to seeing what more balanced version of The Fool will look like in the full game.

Other than that, the testing branch now has two new modes: Blitz, a more bite-sized version where there's no map or gold, and Dread, which appears to be an Ascension+ mode for masochists. Could never be me.

#3947. Xbox Announces Black Friday Sale 2026, Reveals Nine Included Games

Earlier this month, we mentioned that Xbox's Black Friday Sale for 2026 was set to begin on November 19th according to a leak, and now Microsoft has officially announced that it will indeed start showing up as of this Thursday.

The leak mentioned it had a start time of 3pm EST, but Xbox actually says that it'll be 9pm PST / 12pm EST / 5am GMT on November 19th going into November 20th, so you might need to hang around a bit longer until the deals appear.

"The best time to grab a gift for gamers is launching on November 19 at 9 PM PST. During our Black Friday sale, save up to 80% on select XBOX and PC games, and check out discounts on select XBOX accessories."

We also have nine confirmed games for this Xbox Black Friday Sale, which are as follows:

If you're a bit underwhelmed by what you're seeing here, don't worry - over 2,000 games will be included in the full Xbox Black Friday Sale, and despite Xbox suggesting they'll be "up to 80% off", we know from past experience that the sale will include discounts of 90% off and even 95% off for some games.

We'll obviously have a whole bunch of Xbox Black Friday roundups for you beginning later this week on Pure Xbox, but we should also mention that Microsoft is promoting discounts on various Xbox accessories (like controllers and Xbox Design Lab purchases) for the Black Friday period, along with a special Samsung TV deal that includes a free Xbox Nano controller along with two months of Xbox Game Pass Ultimate.

Sit tight, and we'll be back with all the big highlights from the Xbox Black Friday game sale in a couple of days' time!

#3946. Sea Of Stars Is Getting A 'Sunset Edition' Switch 2 Physical And A Gorgeous Final Merch Drop

Sabotage Studio's Sea of Stars is no stranger to a physical release or merch drop, and today, iam8bit has announced that it has one final collection in store.

A brand new Switch 2 physical, the Sea of Stars: Sunset Edition ($49.99), is the star of the show, launching on 2nd April 2027. This one packs the full game and all of its expansions on the cartridge (what a concept!), and comes with some sweet sticker sheets and a download code for the game's soundtrack.

There's a beefier option in the Exclusive Edition, which also boasts an exclusive sleeve and an in-box manual, for those after a little throwback.

The beefiest of the bunch, mind you, is still to come. The Collector's Edition contains all of the goodies outlined above, and throws in a bunch of extra merch too. We're talking a double-sided poster, a tote bag, a reversible bandana, a Rainbow Conch keychain, and seven pins, all housed in a Rainbow Conch Chest. Come on, that's sweet.

The Collector's Edition comes in at a pricey $129.99 (or you can just get the merch for $79.99). All of the above are now available to pre-order from the iam8bit website until 11th January, before shipping in April.

As if all of that wasn't enough, iam8bit has also announced that it has two vinyl LPs in the pipeline, one all about the main game soundtrack, and one featuring the tunes from the Throes of the Watchmaker DLC. You'll also find pre-order information about these on the iam8bit site.

#3945. 40th Anniversary Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks live: where to check for new waves of stock

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Get the biggest gaming news, reviews, and releases straight to your inbox.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Legend of Zelda Nintendo Switch 2 restocks have remained dry over the last week, but more could be on the way shortly. Sites like Amazon and Nintendo have been drip-feeding new handhelds onto the shelves in smaller waves, while stores like Target and GameStop have prioritized in-store options instead.

That means the hunt for the special edition 40th Anniversary handheld marches on, and with the biggest shopping week of the year on the horizon it's likely we'll see a little more action here shortly. Thanksgiving week represents a massive opportunity for retailers to secure eyes on their holiday discounts by also dropping Legend of Zelda Switch 2 stock at the same time.

Only time will tell if everyone is holding off for next week's Black Friday deals, if we spot a new listing or a sniff of stock anywhere across the US or UK, we're bringing it right here to you first.

I've been tracking hard-to-find stock for over six years now, starting with the incredibly limited releases of the PS5 and Xbox Series X. I've been reporting on how retailers operate with high-demand products, from anniversary releases to brand new consoles, ever since then - including the Nintendo Switch 2 itself.

Amazon has been restocking the Legend of Zelda Nintendo Switch 2 in bits and pieces for a little while now. Drops have dried up in recent days, but the little-and-often mantra has definitely been true here in the past.

Ocarina of Time (digital): $54.99 (was $59.99)

Walmart fumbled its pre-orders and hasn't dropped any Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks since. Now, the site seems to have removed its listing for the special edition handheld, with the Pro Controller and carry case either out of stock or monstrously price-inflated. Still, that could all change at any time.

Target ran its own Zelda Switch 2 restocks when Ocarina of Time remake first dropped. It's been quiet since then, though, without a word on when new handhelds or accessories will be available.

Best Buy has been similarly quiet since Ocarina of Time remake launched, opting for an in-person midnight event to celebrate the game (and hand out a few special edition consoles at the same time).

Nintendo itself seems to be one of the more reliable retailers out there. The brand's own store page has been dropping small amounts of handhelds every now and then over the last week, so it's well worth keeping in touch.

GameStop is only running Legend of Zelda Nintendo Switch 2 restocks in stores, so you won't find any online stock here. The store looks like it's about to start running Pro Controller and carry case restocks online, though.

Amazon UK has been a pretty reliable source of Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks in the last few weeks, even if things have slowed down in recent days. Like its US counterpart, the site is dropping a small number of special edition handhelds at a time.

EE has had two Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks since launch day, but the boost here comes from those bundles. The site has previously been offering discounts on Ocarina of Time remake and Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream when bought with the device.

Smyths Toys has seemingly removed its Legend of Zelda Switch 2 listing, which is odd for one of the few UK retailers with the whole collection previously on its site. The Pro Controller page is still up, even if the carry case has also mysteriously vanished here.

Here's the thing with Very. It often bundles up difficult-to-find stock with extra accessories or games to keep resellers at bay. That means you'll be paying a little more here (though still only RRP for everything you're getting) but stock often holds out a lot longer.

Argos was previously offering Legend of Zelda Switch 2 stock ahead of launch, but things look to have run dry now. The store organises its inventory by postcode, though, so it's always worth checking your local area's delivery and collection options.

Currys previously had a listing page up for the Legend of Zelda Switch 2, but it seems to have disappeared now, instead sending us to a generic consoles search page.

Nintendo has also stated more stock is on the way, so you'd expect its own store to be one of the first with fresh handhelds up for grabs.

Very is currently bundling its Legend of Zelda Switch 2s with Ocarina of Time (well it would be if stock was live). Still, that means it's likely these will be a little easier to get hold of when availability drops once again. You're not saving any money on the game itself (unlike EE's supplies), but packaging the game in from the off often deters resellers long enough for actual fans to get to checkout.

Target gave us a fair warning last time it restocked the Legend of Zelda Switch 2. The retailer announced its November 5 and November 6 drops right on the listing page itself. Right now, though, it looks like the store doesn't have anything in the works - at least nothing it wants to shout about just yet.

A jumpscare of Amazon stock just flitted across my screen, but it looks like this is the return of the £499.99 price we were seeing ahead of launch. The Legend of Zelda Nintendo Switch 2 is technically available at the retailer, but it should be noted that the handheld itself carries a £429.99 price tag when sold by reputable sellers. Avoid this one.

Walmart's Legend of Zelda Switch 2 listing page has been out of commission for just over a week now, with no sign of returning. The retailer's mishandling of its pre-orders were originally to blame for its lack of stock, as the store sought to catch up on mistakenly cancelled orders. However, with radio silence and not even a picture of the handheld on the site, things are looking squeaky here.

UK Legend of Zelda stock hunters should be keeping in touch with Argos when new shipments arrive. Competition is significantly lower here - the retailer runs its restocks through local inventory. That means you're only up against those in your local area when new handhelds are available.

GameStop isn't running online Zelda Switch 2 restocks, instead sending customers to their brick and mortar stores. It's well worth checking in with your local, though, stock levels are going to be different across the country and we don't know when those fresh shipments are due in.

EE has been running an additional promotion around its Legend of Zelda Switch 2 stock in the last few weeks. Consoles are available with £10 off the Ocarina of Time remake, £21.49 off Pokemon Pokopia, or £22.08 off Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream. While stock is still currently unavailable, EE has been one of the more active retailers in the last few weeks.

The Zelda Switch 2 restock pattern we're seeing at the moment rewards those in the right place at the right time. Retailers are dropping very small amounts of stock irregularly, so those 'Add to cart' buttons can jump to life at any moment, and die just as quickly. That's why it's so important to make sure you stay signed into retailer accounts throughout your stock hunt.

Getting through to checkout as quickly as possible is the real challenge here, and any clicks you can save signing in, filling out delivery information, and adding payment details can see you fall behind the pack.

The reseller market is rife with inflated prices this week and marketplace sellers are starting to lift those costs on larger retailers as well. That's why it pays to know exactly how much you should be paying for 40th Anniversary Legend of Zelda kit:

While stock itself is still nowhere to be found, GameStop looks like it's opened up the possibility of online Zelda Switch 2 Pro Controller and carry case restocks. The handheld itself is still strictly in-store, but those accessories are listed as 'Coming Soon' or 'Currently Unavailable' online, rather than pointing customers towards their local stores.

Nintendo itself has been one of the more reliable retailers this restock period, and while it's been a little quieter as of late it is running a notification system. Head over to the official Legend of Zelda Switch 2 listing and you'll find a link to the Nintendo Store app. As long as you're signed in, you can add the handheld to your wish list and you'll be notified next time stock drops onto the shelves.

Legend of Zelda Switch 2 | Check stock at Nintendo

Walmart's listings also include third party marketplace sellers, and this is where we often see inflated prices on hard-to-find gadgets. It's happening with the Zelda Pro Controller and has been spotted on the carry case and handheld as well.

This is just a reminder not to pay over MSRP for your Legend of Zelda kit, but to also filter your Walmart search results to those only sold by Walmart itself.

With such a quiet week last week, it makes sense to expect a fresh wave of Legend of Zelda Switch 2 restocks shortly. Retailers have had another week to fill their warehouses now, so it makes sense that those handhelds will be filing onto the shelves soon.

It could be this week, but it's more likely that next week is going to be the big one. With Black Friday nearly upon us, stores are going to want to go bigger at the end of the month.

As teased towards the end of last week, The Blood of Dawnwalker studio Rebel Wolves has updated its PS5 RPG with a new game+ mode, available to download now.

It's a 4.157GB download, and the option to play the game again whilst carrying over your level, skills, and inventory is the main attraction.

Having finished the RPG's epilogue, you'll unlock new game+. The level cap is raised to 100 in your second playthrough, and the difficulty scaling tied to each region is removed. Enemy levels have been adjusted, and they shall have damage multipliers so combat still presents a challenge.

"In NG+, armor, swords, and accessories will have new versions with updated stats while keeping their original names and icons," the blog post reveals. "You can easily recognize these items by their new frames and the NG+ label next to their names (and for NG+ legendary items – a unique red frame)."

New Game+ becomes a new option on the main menu, and begins after selecting your base game save and difficulty level. You'll then get all your gear at the start of the Withering Away quest in the prologue.

#3942. Xbox Series X|S Estimated At 38M Sales, And Here's How That Compares To Other Consoles

They've just celebrated their sixth anniversaries

The Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S officially celebrated their sixth anniversaries back on November 10th, and to mark the occasion, Niko Partners analyst Daniel Ahmad has been looking into a whole bunch of sales estimates.

In a post over on social media, Ahmad estimated that the Series X and S are now at a combined 38 million sales worldwide, and then compared that figure to loads of other consoles that we've seen throughout the years.

The comparison is specifically referencing the sales of each console after six years on the market, so when the Xbox 360 is referenced at 60 million sales, for example, it still racked up another 20+ million until it was discontinued.

As you can see, it doesn't make for great reading overall. Sony has shipped a lot more PS5 consoles than Microsoft has Xbox consoles throughout this generation, and even compared to past Xbox systems, the Series X and S have struggled to keep pace. That said, the original Xbox only racked up around 25m sales, so that one's been beaten at least.

Ahmad also points out that "console players are monetizing at levels significantly higher than any prior gen", so even though hardware sales have been poor for Xbox, content and services revenue has grown massively in recent years.

People will point to this kind of stuff as evidence that Xbox is "failing", but Microsoft is much more interested in the content and services side of things, and that's been a much bigger success for them since the Xbox Series X and S first launched. With Project Helix around the corner though, they'll still hope they can attract a bigger piece of the pie in the hardware space, although that'll be a very tough ask amidst an ongoing component crisis.

@Banjo- Yes, I agree. It's a common mistake to judge a console's success solely by its current sales figures when, in reality, PlayStation is still largely riding on the success and reputation of the PS4 era. For many casual gamers who do not follow the industry closely, PlayStation remains the default choice.

At the same time, the launch of the Xbox Series consoles, combined with some poorly communicated marketing campaigns and Microsoft's multiplatform strategy, certainly didn't help Xbox's image or momentum.

Ironically, it's only toward the end of this generation that the Xbox Series consoles are really starting to show their strengths. It's a shame this is happening so late. That said, I think the current generation will remain relevant for quite a long time, thanks to technologies such as FSR, Microsoft's strong commitment to backward compatibility, a renewed focus on exclusives, and likely the high price of the next generation of hardware.

Another point worth looking at is game sales across the two ecosystems, or even the number of active players. The gap there is nowhere near as large as the difference in console sales would suggest.

That's why I think using hardware sales alone can be misleading. Console sales tell us how many machines have been sold, but they don't necessarily reflect player engagement, software sales, ecosystem revenue, or the actual audience available to a game's publisher.

In my view, metrics such as active users, hours played, software sales, subscription numbers, and overall ecosystem engagement provide a much more accurate picture of the relative strength of each platform.

For all of these reasons, I believe the gap between the two ecosystems is often misunderstood, and looking only at console sales paints a very incomplete picture of the market.

That meant that PC gamers who may have bought an Xbox in the past for games like Halo, Forza, Gears etc now no longer needed to buy. The also spent the latter part and some of this generation telling people they didn't need an Xbox console because 'everything' was an Xbox, their PC, their mobile, their tablet etc. All of which made the Series S/X a pointless purchase to some gamers who already own or prefer to play on PC and can even stream games to their XB1 if they wanted. You don't 'need' to upgrade from an XB1 to play GTA6 for example because you can play via streaming saving you a LOT of money as Consoles have also gone up over the Generation too.

If you had a decent PC rig, you may have wanted an Xbox One for MS exclusives but around 3yrs into that generation, they could buy and play all Xbox games day/date on their PC and therefore had no reason to buy a Series S/X.

Right, has PlayStation been struggling this generation? Absolutely, yes! No doubt about it. That said, PlayStation is only struggling by the standards of the previous generation, and only then because of their chasing Live Service games.

These are the exclusive games that have been on the PS5 and PC (I've included PC because the same is true of Xbox):

Many of those games were nominated for Game of the Year too, and whilst recent times have seen slightly fewer exclusives, they have still had far more than Xbox, and they have been generally of far higher quality too.

I don't understand where you stand when it comes to exclusives because you are championing the fact that Sharma has said we will get more, whilst now apparently saying they are unimportant. You chop and change to suit whatever argument you choose to have on any given day.

We all know exclusives are vital to bringing gamers into an ecosystem. No, they are not the only thing to do that, but they are vital nonetheless, which is why Sony has stopped putting their games on PC too.

As for Xbox not really having exclusives because they are also on PC (a point many seem to overlook), I totally get that it means they are available to way more people than game solely on a PlayStation, but if you think about it, it also goes to show just how badly Xbox first-party games sell when even with a massive number of PC gamers to sell to, Xbox games still barely shift the dial. Just look at E-Day on Steam, which saw an all time peak high of just 31,517! I mean, all those additional people on Steam that have access to E-Day, and the best they can manage is 31,517 (with the peak high for the past 24 hours being just 4,111). Honestly, it's worrying. Anyone that thinks The Coalition is going to be immune from the cuts that Sharma still needs to make in this fiscal year, has a lot more confidence in that than I do.

Honestly though, matey, you always throw in PlayStation whenever someone speaks even remotely critically of Xbox. It's like a reflex action for you to try to diminish PlayStation as if that somehow excuses Xbox. Sony have sold 62% more consoles than Microsoft, yet somehow you think they are doing badly. I totally agree that there is a lot of anger out there about Sony right now, although apparently much of that was actually driven by bots and fake accounts. And Sony's pursuit of Live Service games has been a disaster and has impacted their first-party offerings, but they are still doing better than Xbox, and I say this as someone that is first and foremost an Xbox gamer. I'm just not blind to what's going on...
